analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal tax breaks for large oil companies while preserving them for small independents.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal tax breaks for large oil companies was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on February 10, 2011 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken away a series of tax benefits from major integrated oil companies and other large oil and gas producers — including a manufacturing tax deduction, percentage depletion, credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, immediate deduction of drilling costs, LIFO accounting, and favorable foreign tax credit treatment — while leaving small, independent oil and gas companies untouched. It was never taken up by the committee with jurisdiction over taxes and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: federal revenue that now goes to oil-company tax breaks would instead stay in the Treasury, reducing what other taxpayers must cover, and the playing field tilts slightly away from the largest fossil fuel producers. The bill was written to shield small, independent oil and gas companies from the changes.

how_it_helps.text: It denied large companies the credit for producing oil from marginal wells and the enhanced oil recovery credit — subsidies aimed at keeping marginal wells running.
It ended their ability to immediately deduct intangible drilling and development costs and to use percentage depletion, both of which shield oil production income from tax.
It removed the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil and gas income and blocked LIFO accounting for major integrated oil companies, raising the tax they owe on ordinary income.
It limited foreign tax credits for companies that pay levies to foreign governments in exchange for economic benefits, closing a route oil companies use to reduce U.S. tax on overseas oil income.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies (the household-name giants) and any oil and gas company with over $50 million in gross receipts, which would lose the credits, deductions, and accounting methods the bill repeals. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The tax preferences the bill repealed were permanent features of the tax code; taking them away would raise the after-tax cost of domestic oil and gas production for large companies, and some of that cost could be passed through to consumers at the pump or in utility bills, at least at the margin.

The bill deliberately left small, independent oil and gas companies untouched, which meant the preferences survived for much of the industry and the revenue raised came only from the largest firms — a design choice opponents could fairly call arbitrary and supporters had to defend.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted roughly $20-40 billion of tax preferences enjoyed by the largest oil companies, and the main cost would have fallen on those companies' profits and potentially a modest amount on consumers through prices. The strongest objection is that stripping credits and deductions from oil companies is effectively a tax increase that could raise energy prices; the counter, which the record reflects, is that these preferences let very large firms deduct exploration and production costs in ways ordinary businesses cannot. The bill was never debated or amended in committee, so its real-world design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled it for consideration, so it died there when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Blumenauer introduced the bill on February 10, 2011, joined by 17 original cosponsors including Reps. Markey, Conyers, and George Miller.
The House referred the bill the same day to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies kept their tax credits, deductions, and LIFO accounting. Ordinary taxpayers continue to bear the difference in federal revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil companies, which kept every break

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 10, 2011 to repeal tax breaks for large oil companies.

for.name: 52 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed repealing oil tax preferences during the 112th Congress, in which these provisions were repeatedly debated but never enacted.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose was to strip major integrated and other large oil companies of roughly half a dozen permanent tax preferences, from percentage depletion to LIFO accounting. It never got a hearing or vote, so those preferences survived intact.

industries.industry: Large independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: Producers with over $50 million in gross receipts would have lost the same credits and deductions even though they are not the household-name majors; the preferences were preserved only for small, independent producers.

industries.industry: Small independent oil and gas companies
industries.note: The bill defined its targets carefully so that small, independent producers kept every credit and deduction it took away from the big firms, leaving the rest of the industry's tax treatment fully intact.
